newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian deputies to focus on social spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: Russian deputies to focus on social spending cuts.

text.p: Russia's opposition-dominated parliament was due on Tuesday to focus on government plans to cut housing and social subsidies, key elements of President Boris Yeltsin's efforts to reform the stagnating economy.

Tuesday's session in the Duma lower house of parliament will kick off what is likely to be several days of passionate debate about the government's efforts to cut spending and simplify the notoriously inefficient tax system.

On Wednesday the Duma will review a government request to cut the 1997 budget as required by low tax revenues this year. Then on Thursday the Duma is scheduled to look at a new tax code which its budget committee has already said it does not like.
"Important decisions are expected this week from the State Duma on a package of social measures and on the tax code," Yeltsin's press service said in a statement on Monday.

"The president is closely following the deputies' examination of these issues," it said in remarks clearly aimed at keeping up the pressure on the communist-dominated Duma before it breaks for its summer recess on June 24.
The government wants to cut social spending to those not in genuine need, and do more for people struggling with Russia's transition to a market economy.

For example, the government would like to trim pensions to about seven million Russians of retirement wage who still work and earn more than a certain minimum. It would also like to target child, veteran and housing benefits.
First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais has called Russia's welfare system "fantastically inefficient" and said the government cannot afford but a fraction of its current welfare obligations.
Chubais, who declared more than $300,000 in 1996 income, said even he received housing subsidies because his father was a World War Two veteran.
Yeltsin on Monday urged the Duma to approve the more liberal tax code and big social spending cuts, but he is likely to face stiff resistance.

The government suffered a setback on Monday when the Duma's budget committee issued a non-binding recommendation to the chamber rejecting the new tax code and proposing more piecemeal legislation to address the most pressing problems.
The communist speaker of the Duma, Gennady Seleznyov, warned that the liberal team now in charge of economic policy could fan social tensions in Russia.

"Everything depends on the government. July, August -- these have to be hot months for the government, from the point of view of solving urgent problems that cannot wait until the autumn," Interfax news agency quoted Seleznyov as saying.

The Duma is also angry about government plans to slash the 1997 budget by 108 trillion roubles ($18.8 billion), saying this will hurt the poorest Russians. But the Duma wants to avoid a head-on clash with the government for fear of provoking Yeltsin into calling early parliamentary elections.
Last week parliament and the government set up a special commission to look in detail at where the cuts might fall.
It has until Wednesday to draw up its recommendations, but Itar Tass news agency quoted Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Petrov on Monday as saying the two sides had made no progress so far.
